newsitem.title: USA: Florida governor proposes $42 bln FY 1998 budget.
newsitem.headline: Florida governor proposes $42 bln FY 1998 budget.

text.p: Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles proposed a $42 billion budget fiscal year 1998 Wednesday, calling for a 30 percent increase in education funding and a 10-cents-a-pack hike in the state cigarette tax.

Two months before state lawmakers return for their 1997 legislative session, Gov. Lawton Chiles unveiled his wish list for fiscal 1998, which begins July 1, a 5.5 percent increase over spending for this year.
"I don't feel bad about this budget. I don't feel like, well, we're putting it out there but the state is on a track for disaster," Chiles said. "I think it meets the basic needs of the state."
Chiles' plan calls for increasing the state's education budget to $12.5 billion, an increase of 30 percent over this year.
Spending for welfare and human services would rise 29 percent to $11.9 billion.
To pay for the spending increases, Chiles is relying on an estimated $757 million in additional recurring revenue and cuts of nearly $230 million from current programs.
Among the budget's most controversial items is 10-cents-a-pack increase in the state cigarette tax, a levy that would raise an estimate $121 million a year.
The increase would boost the state's cigarette tax to 44 cents a pack and be used to fund statewide alcohol, drug and tobacco awareness programs aimed at public school students.
"Any time you increase the cost of cigarettes, it is a deterrent for kids because they can spend their money elsewhere," said Beth Labasky, an anti-smoking lobbyist.
Chiles' proposal also calls for nearly $1.04 billion in bonds for environment, education, prisons and transportation projects.
--$502.3 million of Public Education Capital Outlay bonds, which are used to fund school construction.
--$478.4 million of right of way and turnpike construction bonds.
--$300 million of Preservation 2000 bonds, used by the state to purchase environmentally sensitive lands.
--$98.1 million in prison construction bonds, to add 5,912 beds to Florida's burgeoning prison system.

On the economic development front, the proposal calls for workers' compensation tax credits as well as tax credits for targeted industries, defense conversion and electrical use. The total incentive package is worth an estimated $120 million.
